a: Listen, then, you kings
p: Chapter 6 picks up the call to rulers that opened the book (1:1) and turns it into a lesson on wisdom.
b: The book began, "Love righteousness, you who judge the earth" (1:1). After the long scene of judgment in chapters 2 to 5, the speaker turns back to the same audience: kings and judges "of the ends of the earth." The address may be a literary frame, a way of saying that the Jewish wisdom taught here is fit for the rulers of the world; the chapter page gives both readings. The first readers, Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt, lived under Ptolemaic or Roman rulers and saw ruler worship around them (see the book's front page). This chapter tells such rulers that their power is on loan from Israel's God.

a: your power was given to you by the Lord
t: Compared with the Bible: power comes from God
p: Wisdom agrees with Daniel, Proverbs and Paul: a ruler's power is given by God, and God will ask for an account.
b: Agrees. Daniel says God "removes kings and he sets kings up" (Daniel 2:21). Paul writes, "There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1), and Jesus tells Pilate he would have no power "if it had not been granted to you from above" (John 19:11). Goes beyond in one point: Wisdom stresses that power given by God makes a ruler God's servant (6:4), so the powerful face a harsher test (6:5–8). The Bible shows the same pattern in the prophets' words to kings, but does not state it as a rule. For the churches that count the book as Scripture this is God's word to rulers; for others it is teaching that matches Romans 13.

a: servants of his kingdom
p: The Greek word is the one for an official or an attendant, not a slave.
b: Hypēretai are assistants or officials: the word is used for a court attendant and, in Luke 1:2, for "servants of the word." Here earthly kings are pictured as officers in God's own kingdom. Their thrones are posts in his administration. The idea answers the royal ideology of the Hellenistic kings, who presented themselves as saviors and even gods (see the topic on ruler worship).
orig: ὑπηρέται ὄντες τῆς αὐτοῦ βασιλείας (hypēretai ontes tēs autou basileias)

a: but the powerful will be powerfully examined
p: The verb means to examine or test. The KJV and the Latin say instead that the powerful will be 'tormented'.
b: The Greek repeats one root: dynatoi dynatōs, "the powerful, powerfully." The verb etazō is the simple form of the verb in 6:3, "he will examine" (exetasei). The KJV has "mightily tormented," and the Latin tormenta patientur, "they will suffer torments." The Plain English Translation keeps the sense of examining, because the verses around it speak of searching and inquiry (6:3, 6:8). The point is the same either way: the greater the power, the stricter the account.
orig: δυνατοὶ δὲ δυνατῶς ἐτασθήσονται (dynatoi de dynatōs etasthēsontai)

a: The Master of all will not draw back before anyone's face
p: The Greek idiom 'draw back before a face' means to show partiality, a theme of the Law and the New Testament.
b: To "respect a face" is the Bible's idiom for favoritism. The Law forbids it to judges: "Do not play favorites" (Deuteronomy 16:19). Job says God "does not even take the side of princes / or prefer the rich over the poor, / since every one of them is something his hands made" (Job 34:19), the same reason Wisdom gives. Peter says, "God does not play favorites" (Acts 10:34), and Paul reminds masters that with their Lord "there is no favoritism" (Ephesians 6:9).

a: you absolute rulers
p: Greek tyrannoi gives English 'tyrant'. The Plain English Translation says 'absolute rulers', its one rendering of the word in this book.
b: The Greek is tyrannoi, the word behind English "tyrant." In English a tyrant is a cruel ruler, but these are the rulers the chapter is trying to win to wisdom (6:9–11). The Plain English Translation uses "absolute rulers" for the word here, at 6:21 and at 8:15, where it comes with "dreaded." Other books on the site keep "tyrant" where the story shows cruelty, as for Antiochus' men in 2 Maccabees 4:25 and 7:27.
orig: ὦ τύραννοι (ō tyrannoi)

a: will be made holy
p: The Greek uses the same root three times: those who keep holy things holily will be made holy.
b: The line plays on one root: hosiōs "in a holy way," ta hosia "the holy things," hosiōthēsontai "they will be made holy." Hosios is the Greek Bible's usual word for the Hebrew chasid, the loyal and devout person. The "holy things" are probably God's laws (6:4, 6:18). Those who have learned them "will have an answer ready" (Greek apologia, a defense in court) at the judgment of 6:5.
orig: οἱ γὰρ φυλάξαντες ὁσίως τὰ ὅσια ὁσιωθήσονται (hoi gar phylaxantes hosiōs ta hosia hosiōthēsontai)

a: Wisdom shines and never fades
t: When is it 'Wisdom' with a capital?
p: From 6:12 the Plain English Translation writes 'Wisdom' with a capital wherever she acts as a person; Greek has no capitals to decide it.
b: Greek manuscripts do not mark capital letters, so the choice is the translator's. The Plain English Translation writes "Wisdom" where sophia acts or is described as a person: she goes looking for people, sits at the gate and has laws (6:12–22), goes before good things (7:12), crafts all things and is a craftswoman (7:22; 8:6), is a bride (8:2–18), sits beside God's thrones (9:4, 9:9–10) and saves and rescues the righteous (9:18; 10:1–21). It writes "wisdom" where the word means the quality or learning a person gains (6:9, 6:23; 7:7; 9:6, 9:17), and at 9:2, where "by your wisdom" stands beside "by your word" (9:1) as God's own power at work rather than as a figure who acts. The line is not sharp in the Greek, which moves freely between the two. The picture of Wisdom as a woman comes from Proverbs, where she calls out in the streets (Proverbs 1:20–33; 8–9).
orig: σοφία (sophia)

a: never fades
p: Amarantos was the word for flowers that never wilt; 1 Peter uses it for the inheritance and the wreath kept in heaven.
b: The amaranth was a flower thought never to wither, and amarantos means "unfading." Wisdom is compared with something that never loses its color. Peter uses the same family of words for the believer's inheritance that "cannot wither" (1 Peter 1:4, amarantos) and the "wreath of glory that never withers" (1 Peter 5:4, amarantinos).
orig: ἀμάραντος (amarantos)

a: sitting at his gates
p: In Proverbs Wisdom shouts at the city gates; here she waits quietly at the seeker's own door.
b: Proverbs pictures Wisdom shouting "next to the gates, at the mouth of the town" (Proverbs 8:3) and promising, "those who hunt hard for me will find me" (Proverbs 8:17). Wisdom of Solomon turns this around: she is already sitting at the seeker's door before he is up. The gate was the town's courthouse and meeting place, so the picture may also mean that a ruler who rises early finds Wisdom ready where he hears cases.

a: The very start of her is a true longing for discipline
p: Verses 17 to 20 are a chain: each step's last word starts the next, from longing to a kingdom.
b: Greek teachers called this figure a sorites, a "heap" argument: each clause picks up the word the last one ended with. Desire for discipline, care for discipline, love, keeping laws, attention to laws, incorruption, nearness to God, a kingdom. The conclusion (6:20) jumps from the start to the end: longing for wisdom lifts a person to a kingdom. Paul builds a chain of the same kind in Romans 5:3–5, and 2 Peter 1:5–7 another. The "kingdom" in Wisdom is both the earthly rule the kings already have and the reign of the righteous with God, which the book has already promised (3:8; 5:16).

a: discipline
p: Paideia means a child's whole upbringing: teaching and correction. The Plain English Translation says 'discipline', as in Proverbs.
b: Paideia covers the whole upbringing of a child: lessons, training and correction. The Plain English Translation renders it "discipline" here and in 6:18 and 7:14, and the verb paideuō "discipline" in 6:11 and 6:25, as the site does for the same Greek word in the rest of the book (3:5; 11:9; 12:22) and for the Hebrew musar that it renders in Proverbs: "for knowing wisdom and discipline" (Proverbs 1:2). In these chapters the sense is mostly teaching and training, not punishment: the learner longs for it and is "disciplined" by the speaker's words (6:11, 6:25).
orig: παιδεία (paideia)

a: the guarantee of incorruption
p: Aphtharsia means not decaying. The Plain English Translation keeps it apart from athanasia, 'immortality' (8:13, 8:17).
b: The book uses two words for the life that death cannot touch: aphtharsia, "incorruption," the state of not decaying (2:23; 6:18–19), and athanasia, "immortality," not dying (3:4; 8:13, 8:17; 15:3). Many English versions use "immortality" for both. The Plain English Translation keeps them apart so the reader can see which Greek word stands where. Paul uses the same pair in 1 Corinthians 15:53: the perishable must put on incorruption, and the mortal immortality. Here incorruption comes from keeping Wisdom's laws, and it brings a person "close to God" (6:19), the hope of 3:1–9.
orig: βεβαίωσις ἀφθαρσίας (bebaiōsis aphtharsias)

a: I will keep no mysteries hidden from you
p: Greek mystery cults kept their rites for initiates. Solomon promises to tell everything openly.
b: The mystery cults of the Greek world, such as that of Demeter at Eleusis, kept their rites secret from outsiders. Wisdom of Solomon uses their language (8:4 calls Wisdom an "initiate" of God's knowledge), but turns it inside out: the speaker will "bring the knowledge of her out into the open." Envy, which hoards knowledge, has no share in wisdom (6:23; compare 7:13). Paul speaks the same way of God's wisdom "in a mystery" now made known (1 Corinthians 2:7).

a: the world's safety
p: Sōtēria means safety or rescue. Here it is the welfare of the world, which wise people keep safe.
b: The Greek is sōtēria kosmou, word for word "salvation of the world," the same words a Christian would use of Christ (John 4:42 calls him "the Savior of the world"). Here it has its everyday political sense: a country is safe when many of its people are wise, as a people stands firm under a sensible king. The KJV's "welfare of the world" is close.
orig: σωτηρία κόσμου (sōtēria kosmou)

a: I too am a mortal
p: The speaker is plainly Solomon, but the book never names him. The book's front page sets out who wrote it.
b: From here to the end of chapter 9 one man speaks: a king who prayed for wisdom, was told to build the temple and speaks of his father's thrones (7:7; 9:7–8, 9:12). The details fit Solomon, and the Greek title calls the book his, but the text never uses his name. Writing in the voice of a famous figure was a common way of teaching in the ancient world. The book's front page sets out the views on who wrote it and when.

a: the first-formed man
p: Greek prōtoplastos, 'first-shaped', is Adam, shaped from the ground in Genesis 2:7. Chapter 10 begins with him.
b: Genesis says, "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7). Wisdom calls him gēgenēs prōtoplastos, "the earth-born, first-formed one," and uses prōtoplastos again at 10:1. Paul says, "The first man came from the earth and was made of dust" (1 Corinthians 15:47). The point of 7:1–6 is that even a king is made of the same earth as everyone.
orig: γηγενοῦς ἀπόγονος πρωτοπλάστου (gēgenous apogonos prōtoplastou)

a: over a time of ten months
p: The verse counts ten months in the womb and pictures the child set firm in blood, as Job pictures milk thickening into cheese.
b: The verse gives ten months as the time in the womb; it does not say how the months were counted. It also pictures the child "set firm in blood" from the man's seed. Job uses a like picture for God forming a child: "Like milk you poured me out, did you not? / Like cheese you made me thicken" (Job 10:10). The point of 7:1–6 is that a king is formed in the womb like everyone else.

a: the pleasure that goes with sleep
p: A delicate way of speaking of a husband and wife sleeping together.
b: The Greek hēdonēs hypnō synelthousēs is "pleasure coming together with sleep": the pleasure of the marriage bed, followed by sleep. The KJV, "the pleasure that came with sleep," keeps the wording. The sense is not shameful; the writer's point is only that a king is conceived like everyone else.
orig: ἡδονῆς ὕπνῳ συνελθούσης (hēdonēs hypnō synelthousēs)

a: Everyone enters life by one door and leaves it by the same
t: One way in, one way out
p: Job and Ecclesiastes say the same: everyone comes out of the womb with nothing and goes out with nothing.
b: "Naked I came out from my mother's womb, / and naked I will return there" (Job 1:21). "Just as he came out of his mother's womb, naked, so he will go back, going the way he came" (Ecclesiastes 5:15). Wisdom applies the old truth to a king: his birth (7:1–5) and his death are the same as any slave's. What sets him apart is not his birth but the wisdom he prayed for (7:7).

a: So I prayed, and I was given understanding
p: This recalls Solomon's request for wisdom in 1 Kings 3, told from Solomon's side; the prayer itself comes in chapter 9.
b: In 1 Kings 3:5–14 God appears to Solomon in a dream and says "Ask," Solomon asks for "a heart that listens, so he can judge your people" (1 Kings 3:9), and God gives him wisdom and also the riches he did not ask for (1 Kings 3:13). Wisdom of Solomon tells the story in the first person, without naming a place: he prayed, and understanding came; he preferred her to thrones and wealth (7:8–10), and wealth came with her (7:11). The full prayer is given in 9:1–18. James draws the lesson for everyone: "If any of you is short of wisdom, let him ask God for it" (James 1:5).

a: a spirit of wisdom
p: The same phrase is used of Joshua, of the Messiah in Isaiah 11, and in Paul's prayer in Ephesians.
b: Joshua "was filled with a spirit of wisdom" when Moses laid hands on him (Deuteronomy 34:9). Isaiah says of the coming king, "The LORD's Spirit will come to rest on him, / a spirit of wisdom and understanding" (Isaiah 11:2), and Paul prays that God "would give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation" (Ephesians 1:17). In this book wisdom is itself a spirit (1:6; 7:22), so the phrase means more than a wise attitude: wisdom comes to the king as a living power from God.

a: is a little sand
p: Proverbs says wisdom is worth more than red coral and gold; here gold is only sand beside her.
b: "For wisdom is better than red coral; / of all the things people want, none is her equal" (Proverbs 8:11; compare Proverbs 3:14–15; Job 28:15–19). Wisdom of Solomon pushes the comparison further: gold is sand and silver is mud. Sand is also the measure of Solomon's wisdom in 1 Kings: God gave him "a heart as broad as the sand along the edge of the sea" (1 Kings 4:29).

a: friendship with God
p: Abraham and Moses were called God's friends; Wisdom says anyone who uses her treasure becomes one (also 7:27).
b: Isaiah calls Israel the "offspring of Abraham, who loved me" (Isaiah 41:8), and James says Abraham "was called the friend of God" (James 2:23). God spoke to Moses "as anyone talks with a close companion" (Exodus 33:11). Wisdom of Solomon widens this: through Wisdom any person can be God's friend (7:27). Jesus tells his disciples, "I have called you friends" (John 15:15).

a: God grant that I speak as I ought
p: The Greek verb is a wish, 'may God grant'. The Latin and the KJV make it a statement: 'God has granted me'.
b: Swete's Greek has the optative dōē, the form of a wish or a prayer: may God grant it. The Vulgate reads dedit, "he gave," and the Douay and the KJV follow that sense ("God hath granted me"). The Plain English Translation follows the Greek. As a wish it fits the humble tone of 7:1–6: the speaker does not claim to have spoken well already but prays that he will. See the variant on "what has been given."
orig: ἐμοὶ δὲ δῴη ὁ θεὸς εἰπεῖν κατὰ γνώμην (emoi de dōē ho theos eipein kata gnōmēn)

a: how the world is put together and how the elements work
p: Verses 17 to 20 list the sciences of a Greek school: cosmology, the calendar, astronomy, zoology, psychology, botany.
b: 1 Kings says Solomon "talked about trees ... about beasts and birds, about creatures that creep, and about fish" (1 Kings 4:33). Wisdom turns that into the full course of Greek learning: the structure of the cosmos (systasis kosmou), the working of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire), the calendar and the solstices, the cycles of years, the positions of the stars, the nature of animals, human reasoning, and the healing powers of roots. The "elements" (stoicheia) are the same word Paul uses in Galatians 4:3 and Colossians 2:8. The point is that true knowledge of nature is God's gift (7:15–16), not a rival to faith.

a: how the sun turns back at the solstices
p: Tropai, 'turnings', are the solstices, when the sun seems to stop and turn back; the word gives English 'tropics'.
b: At midsummer and midwinter the sun's rising point stops moving along the horizon and turns back. The Greeks called these the tropai, "turnings," and the lines of latitude where the sun stands overhead at those times are still called the tropics. James may echo the same word when he says God has "no shadow cast by turning" (James 1:17, tropē).
orig: τροπῶν ἀλλαγάς (tropōn allagas)

a: the positions of the stars
p: The verse names the stars' positions, knowledge used for the calendar. The book condemns star worship (13:2).
b: The Greek asterōn theseis is "the positions of the stars," the same word as in 7:29, "above every position of the stars." Wisdom names only the stars' positions and says nothing of reading fates from them. Later the book rebukes those who took "the circle of the stars" for gods (13:2). Genesis gives the lights in the sky the job to "mark the appointed times, the days and the years" (Genesis 1:14).
orig: ἀστέρων θέσεις (asterōn theseis)

a: the force of the winds
p: Pneumata can mean winds or spirits. Some read 'the power of spirits', and Jewish legend made Solomon master of demons.
b: Pneumatōn bias is "the violence of pneumata," a word that means both winds and spirits. In a list of natural sciences, between wild animals and human thoughts, "winds" fits well, and the KJV has "the violence of winds." But "spirits" is possible, and later Jewish and Christian legend made Solomon the master of demons, a tradition behind the Testament of Solomon, a writing in no church's Bible. The Plain English Translation follows the natural-science reading. Both senses of the word stand side by side in John 3:8.
orig: πνευμάτων βίας (pneumatōn bias)

a: the powers in roots
p: The healing powers of roots and herbs were part of ancient medicine; Sirach praises the physician and his remedies.
b: Plants and their roots were a main source of medicine in the ancient world. Wisdom counts knowing their powers as a gift of God to the wise king. Sirach says much the same when it praises the doctor and the remedies God made grow from the earth (Sirach 38:1–8).

a: who crafted all things
p: Technitis, 'craftswoman', is a feminine form: Wisdom is God's artisan, as in Proverbs 8:30.
b: Technitis is a woman skilled in a craft (the masculine technitēs is used of God the builder in Hebrews 11:10). The book calls Wisdom this again in 8:6, where some codices have the masculine instead (see the variant there). It recalls Proverbs 8:30, where Wisdom says, "I was at his side, a craftsman" (Hebrew amon, a word whose sense is debated). In Wisdom she is the one through whom God made all things, which is why she can teach the king how they are made (7:17–21).
orig: ἡ γὰρ πάντων τεχνῖτις (hē gar pantōn technitis)

a: she has in her a spirit
p: The spirit in Wisdom is described with twenty adjectives and one phrase: three times seven.
b: Counting the Greek, 7:22–23 gives twenty adjectives (from "thinks" to "watching over all") and one participle phrase ("making its way through every spirit"), twenty-one in all: three, the number of fullness, times seven, the number of completeness. Many of the words come from Greek philosophy. The Stoics taught that a fine, fiery pneuma runs through the whole universe and holds it together; "fine," "quick-moving" and "making its way through" are their language. But Wisdom is not the world's soul here: she is "a vapor rising from God's power" (7:25), distinct from the world she pervades. Compare the sevenfold Spirit of Revelation 1:4.

a: one of a kind
p: The word is the one John uses of the Son, 'an only son' (John 1:14). It means unique, the only one of its kind.
b: Monogenēs means "the only one of its kind," and of a child, an only child. John uses it of Jesus: "the kind of glory an only son has from his father" (John 1:14; compare John 3:16). Here Wisdom's spirit is unique and yet "many-sided" (polymeres), the next word: one in itself, present in many ways. Hebrews 1:1 uses the root of polymeres for the "many parts" in which God spoke before he spoke in a Son.
orig: μονογενές, πολυμερές (monogenes, polymeres)

a: She is a vapor rising from God's power
p: Atmis is steam or vapor rising from something; aporroia is an outflow, as water from a spring.
b: Two pictures describe how Wisdom comes from God. Atmis is vapor or steam, like breath on a cold day or mist rising from water: it is from the source and like it, but not separate from it. Aporroia is a flowing out, an emanation, like water from a spring or light from a lamp. Both pictures make Wisdom come from God and resemble him; how close the likeness is became a question in the debates over the Son (see the note on 7:26, "7:25–26 in the fight over the Son"). The Latin has vapor and emanatio. Origen quotes these words and those of 7:26 in his chapter "On Christ" (On First Principles 1.2.9) and explains them of the Son.
orig: ἀτμὶς γάρ ἐστιν τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ δυνάμεως, καὶ ἀπόρροια (atmis gar estin tēs tou theou dynameōs, kai aporroia)

a: She is a radiance of eternal light
t: Radiance: the word Hebrews uses of the Son
p: Apaugasma, 'radiance', occurs in Swete's Greek Old Testament only here, and in the New Testament only in Hebrews 1:3.
b: Hebrews says of the Son: "He is the brightness that shines out from God's glory and the exact stamp of his being" (Hebrews 1:3). The Greek is apaugasma, the word used here; in Swete's Greek Old Testament it occurs nowhere else. Colossians says of Christ, "He is the image of the God who cannot be seen" (Colossians 1:15), and 7:26 calls Wisdom "an image of his goodness." Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). The shared words suggest that the New Testament writers drew on the Jewish picture of Wisdom that this verse holds to say who the Son is. Whether they knew this book itself cannot be shown from the wording alone; the words may have been common in Jewish teaching.
orig: ἀπαύγασμα γάρ ἐστιν φωτὸς ἀιδίου (apaugasma gar estin phōtos aidiou)

a: a stainless mirror of God's working
p: Ancient mirrors were polished bronze, and any spot spoiled the image. Wisdom shows God's activity perfectly.
b: A mirror in the ancient world was a disk of polished metal, which tarnished easily (Paul's "we see in a mirror, dimly," 1 Corinthians 13:12). A spotless mirror gives back the true image. Wisdom reflects God's energeia, his working or activity. The Vulgate reads "mirror of God's majesty," and the KJV "mirror of the power of God."
orig: ἔσοπτρον ἀκηλίδωτον τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνεργείας (esoptron akēlidōton tēs tou theou energeias)

a: She is a radiance of eternal light
t: 7:25-26 in the fight over the Son
p: Origen read these verses of the Son; in the Arian controversy the radiance image became a key Nicene argument.
b: Origen, in the chapter "On Christ" of On First Principles (1.2.9), quotes Wisdom 7:25–26 in full and explains each phrase of the Son. A century later, in the fight with the followers of Arius, whose saying Athanasius quotes as "There was once when He was not," Athanasius argued from the radiance image of Hebrews 1:3, this verse's word: the Son is "the eternal Radiance of a Light which is eternal," and light is never without its radiance, so the Son never was not (Orations against the Arians 1.13; 1.20). The Arian side is known here only as Athanasius reports it. The Proverbs 8 card asks the related question of whether Wisdom is the eternal Son; see the card at Proverbs 8.

a: she makes all things new
p: Wisdom renews everything while staying the same; in Revelation the one on the throne says the same of himself.
b: The Greek ta panta kainizei, "she makes all things new," is very close to the words of Revelation 21:5: "Look, I am making all things new." Wisdom renews the world from day to day while "she stays as she is," the Greek idea that the divine is unchanging and yet active. Revelation uses the thought for the new creation at the end.

a: friends of God and prophets
p: The book links wisdom and prophecy: Wisdom enters holy souls in every age; chapter 10 then shows who they were.
b: In the Hebrew Bible wisdom and prophecy are mostly separate gifts: the sage teaches, the prophet speaks God's word. Here the two meet. In every generation Wisdom crosses into holy souls and makes them prophets, and chapter 10 lists them, from Adam to Moses. Jesus speaks of "God's Wisdom" sending prophets (Luke 11:49), which suggests that Jews of his time could speak of Wisdom as the one who sends the prophets.

a: God loves nothing except
p: The Greek says flatly that God loves 'nothing except' the one who lives with Wisdom. It is a strong way of praising her.
b: The words are absolute: outhen agapa ho theos ei mē, "God loves nothing except." Elsewhere the book says that God "loves all that exists" (11:24) and hates nothing he made. So the line is not a doctrine that God hates the unwise. It is a way of saying that the life lived with Wisdom is what God delights in above all. "Makes his home with" (synoikounta) is the word for a husband living with a wife, which prepares for the bride picture of 8:2.
orig: οὐθὲν γὰρ ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεὸς εἰ μὴ τὸν σοφίᾳ συνοικοῦντα (outhen gar agapa ho theos ei mē ton sophia synoikounta)

a: She stretches out in strength from one end to the other
p: The Latin of this verse is woven into the Advent antiphon O Sapientia, one of the Great 'O' Antiphons.
b: The Latin of this verse reads attingit ergo a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit omnia suaviter. Its words are woven into the antiphon O Sapientia, one of the Great "O" Antiphons of Advent, sung at the Magnificat at Vespers. The Cantus Database gives its text from a Vienna manuscript (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. 1799**) as O sapientia quae ex ore altissimi prodisti attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter suaviter disponensque omnia veni ad docendum nos viam prudentiae. In the site's own English: "O Wisdom, you who came out from the mouth of the Most High, reaching from end to end mightily and ordering all things sweetly: come to teach us the way of prudence." The antiphon joins this verse to Sirach 24:3, where Wisdom says, "I came out of the Most High's mouth," and it calls on Wisdom to come.

a: I wanted to bring her home as my bride
p: The king courts Wisdom as a wife: he loves her, brings her home, lives with her and rests with her.
b: Chapter 8 is a love story. The verb agagesthai (8:2, 8:9) is the Greek term for a man bringing a bride into his house; symbiōsis, "living together" (8:3, 8:9, 8:16), is a word for married life; and the king is her erastēs, "lover" (8:2). Proverbs had already told young men to love Wisdom and hold her close (Proverbs 4:6–8; 7:4). Solomon, whose many wives turned his heart away (1 Kings 11:1–4), is here pictured as the man who wanted only one bride.

a: Her life shared with God
p: The same word for married life is used of Wisdom and God: she 'lives with God', and he loves her.
b: Symbiōsin theou echousa, "having a shared life with God." The writer uses the same word for the king's life with Wisdom (8:9, 8:16). The picture is a way of saying how close Wisdom is to God, nearer than any creature, without making her a second God. Proverbs says she was "at his side" (Proverbs 8:30).
orig: συμβίωσιν θεοῦ ἔχουσα (symbiōsin theou echousa)

a: She shares the secret knowledge of God
p: Mystis is the word for one initiated into a mystery cult. Wisdom is 'initiated' into what God knows.
b: A mystis was a person initiated into the secret rites of a Greek mystery cult. The writer borrows the word to say that Wisdom shares God's own knowledge, and in the same breath (hairetis, "one who chooses") that she takes part in choosing what God will do. The sense of hairetis is not certain: the Latin has electrix, "chooser," as the Plain English Translation does, while the KJV has "a lover of his works." Compare 6:22, where the speaker refuses to keep her mysteries secret.
orig: μύστις γάρ ἐστιν τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπιστήμης, καὶ αἱρετὶς τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ (mystis gar estin tēs tou theou epistēmēs, kai hairetis tōn ergōn autou)

a: She teaches self-control and understanding, / righteousness and courage
p: These are the four main virtues of Greek philosophy since Plato. Christians later called them the cardinal virtues.
b: Self-control (sōphrosynē), understanding or prudence (phronēsis), righteousness or justice (dikaiosynē) and courage (andreia) are the four virtues Plato set out in the Republic, and the Stoics taught them as the four main virtues. The writer claims them for Wisdom: a Jew in Alexandria did not need to go to the Greek schools for virtue. Christian teachers later called these four the "cardinal" (hinge) virtues, beside faith, hope and love. The Plain English Translation keeps "righteousness" for dikaiosynē, as everywhere in the book, though in this list it is the Greek virtue of justice.
orig: σωφροσύνην γὰρ καὶ φρόνησιν ἐκδιδάσκει, δικαιοσύνην καὶ ἀνδρείαν (sōphrosynēn gar kai phronēsin ekdidaskei, dikaiosynēn kai andreian)

a: the answers to riddles
p: The queen of Sheba came to test Solomon with riddles; Proverbs is written to explain the riddles of the wise.
b: "So she came to put him to the test with riddles" (1 Kings 10:1). Proverbs is written "for understanding a proverb and a figure, / what the wise say and the riddles they pose" (Proverbs 1:6). Wisdom adds knowledge of the past and future and of "signs and wonders," which prepares for the signs and wonders of the Exodus in 10:16.

a: young as I am
p: Solomon calls himself 'only a youngster' in 1 Kings 3:7; here Wisdom will make the elders respect him.
b: "I am only a youngster. I don't know how to come and go" (1 Kings 3:7). In 9:5 the speaker says he is weak and short-lived. Here, looking forward, he imagines Wisdom winning him honor from the elders, as 1 Kings 3:28 says all Israel "feared the king" when they saw his judgment. Elders putting a hand over the mouth (8:12) is the gesture of Job 29:9, where princes fall silent before Job.

a: Through her I will gain immortality
p: Two kinds of 'immortality' may be meant: an undying name among people, and life with God after death.
b: The second line speaks of "a memory that lasts forever," the immortality of fame that Greek and Jewish writers alike prized. But the book has already said that "the souls of the righteous are in God's hand" and that their hope is "full of immortality" (3:1, 3:4). So athanasia here can be read in both senses: Wisdom gives a good name on earth and life with God beyond death. In 8:17 the speaker says that "in being joined to Wisdom there is immortality." On whether the soul is immortal by nature or by God's gift, see the card at chapter 3.
orig: ἕξω δι᾽ αὐτὴν ἀθανασίαν (hexō di' autēn athanasian)

a: a good soul was given me as my share
p: The verb means to receive by lot. A good soul was his portion, as if souls were handed out.
b: Elachon is from lanchanō, to get something by lot, as land or an office was given out by drawing lots. The speaker says a good soul was his share. Read alone, the line suggests that the body is the person ("I") and the soul is something he received. The next verse corrects this.
orig: ψυχῆς τε ἔλαχον ἀγαθῆς (psychēs te elachon agathēs)

a: Or better, since I was good, I came into a body without stain
t: Did his soul exist before his body?
p: It seems to say his good self existed first and then entered a body. Readers take it in four ways.
b: "Or better" (mallon de) corrects 8:19: the true "I" is the soul, which, being good, came into a body. Readings: (1) Pre-existence: the soul lived before the body and entered it, as in Plato. (2) Not a doctrine: the writer only means that the person, soul first, is the true self, and he is not thinking about when souls begin. (3) Creation of the soul: God creates each soul and joins it to its body, so "I came" means only that the soul is the person. (4) The Latin reads "since I was more good," a reading that moves the stress from the order of soul and body to the goodness. The churches' teaching on where souls come from is on the card below.
orig: μᾶλλον δὲ ἀγαθὸς ὢν ἦλθον εἰς σῶμα ἀμίαντον (mallon de agathos ōn ēlthon eis sōma amianton)

a: I came into a body without stain
t: Compared with the Bible: a soul before the body
p: If it means the soul existed before the body, it goes beyond the 66 books, and many think it conflicts.
b: Goes beyond. The Hebrew Bible pictures a human being as one living whole: "the man became a living being" when God breathed into the dust (Genesis 2:7). Jeremiah 1:5 ("Before I shaped you in the belly, I knew you") speaks of God's knowledge and choosing, not of a soul living before the body. Conflicts, if read as Origen taught it, with later church teaching: the fifteen anathemas against Origen usually assigned to the Second Council of Constantinople (553) begin by condemning "the fabulous pre-existence of souls." Whether that council adopted them, or a synod at Constantinople in 543, is disputed (Percival's excursus in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers). Read the other way, as naming the soul as the true self, the verse does not conflict. See the card on this chapter.

a: I would not win her any other way, unless God gave her
p: Enkratēs can mean 'in possession of' or 'self-controlled'. The Latin chose 'continent', and Augustine built on it.
b: The Greek enkratēs means "having power over, in possession of" (here, of Wisdom), and also "self-controlled." The Greek gives "gave" no object; the Plain English Translation supplies "her" from the chapter, where he wants Wisdom as his bride and knows she is God's gift. The KJV ("obtain her") takes the same sense. The Vulgate took the second: non possem esse continens, nisi Deus det, "I could not be continent unless God gave it." Augustine quotes it in his Confessions: "none can be continent unless Thou give it" (6.11.20), and again "no man can be continent unless Thou give it" (10.31.45). In 10.29.40, the passage of his prayer "Give what You command, and command what You will," he quotes the verse in the other sense: "I could not otherwise obtain her, except God gave her me." For Augustine the Latin verse taught that even self-control is God's gift.
orig: ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλως ἔσομαι ἐγκρατὴς ἐὰν μὴ ὁ θεὸς δῷ (hoti ouk allōs esomai enkratēs ean mē ho theos dō)

a: God of the fathers, Lord of your mercy
p: Chapter 9 recalls Solomon's prayer in 1 Kings 3 and 2 Chronicles 1, and sets it after the command to build the temple.
b: In Kings and Chronicles Solomon begins with God's "great loyal love" to David (1 Kings 3:6; 2 Chronicles 1:8) and asks, "So now give me wisdom and knowledge" (2 Chronicles 1:10). Here the prayer opens with God's mercy (eleos, the Greek Bible's word for hesed) and his creation, asks "Give me Wisdom" (9:4), names his weakness (9:5), and recalls that he must judge the people (9:7, 9:12; 1 Kings 3:9). But it also says God told him to build a sanctuary (9:8), which is not part of the dream at Gibeon in 1 Kings 3. The command to build comes in David's words to Solomon, "the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the holy place" (1 Chronicles 28:10), with the pattern David gave him (1 Chronicles 28:11–19), and in Solomon's own words, "Your son ... is the one who will build the house for my name" (1 Kings 5:5). The book names no place or time for the prayer. The Greek has "God of the fathers," with no "my." Solomon is never named here either; see 7:1.
orig: Θεὲ πατέρων καὶ Κύριε τοῦ ἐλέους σου (Thee paterōn kai Kyrie tou eleous sou)
r: 1 Kings 3:6–9; 2 Chronicles 1:8–10; 1 Chronicles 28:6–19; 1 Kings 5:5; 1 Kings 8:17–20; 7:1; 1 Chronicles 29:18–19

a: by your word you made all things
t: Made by word and by wisdom
p: God made all things by his word (9:1) and formed humankind by his wisdom (9:2): two ways of naming God's creative power.
b: "The heavens were made by the LORD's word" (Psalm 33:6), and "You made every one of them with wisdom" (Psalm 104:24). The prayer puts the two lines side by side, as Hebrew poetry does: word and wisdom are both God's own power at work in creation. John 1:1–3 later says all things came to be through the Word. Readers have asked whether the writer thought of the word (logos) as a person, as Philo did. In this book it stays God's spoken word; it is personified only at 18:15.

a: who sits beside you on your thrones
p: Wisdom is God's paredros, the one who sits beside; the Greek says 'your thrones' in the plural.
b: Paredros is "one who sits beside." In 6:14 Wisdom is found as the paredros of the seeker's gates, waiting there; here she sits beside God. The plural "thrones" may be a plural of majesty, or a hint of one throne shared by two. Hebrews 1:3 says the Son "took his seat at the right hand of the Majesty in the heights."
orig: τὴν τῶν σῶν θρόνων πάρεδρον σοφίαν (tēn tōn sōn thronōn paredron sophian)

a: from among your children
p: Paides means both children and servants; the next verse calls the king God's slave.
b: Paides can mean "children" or "servants," as at 2:13, where the righteous man calls himself a pais of the Lord. Since Israel is God's son in this book (18:13) and the righteous are his children (2:13, 2:18; 5:5), the Plain English Translation says "children"; "servants" is just as possible and fits the next line, "I am your slave."
orig: ἐκ παίδων σου (ek paidōn sou)

a: the son of your servant girl
p: The phrase comes from the Psalms: a slave born to a slave woman in the household.
b: "I am your servant, your servant girl's son" (Psalm 116:16; compare Psalm 86:16). A slave born to a slave woman in the household belonged to the master from birth. Doulos is "slave"; the Plain English Translation follows the site's rule of "servant or slave by context," and here the speaker humbles himself as far as he can.
orig: ὅτι ἐγὼ δοῦλος σὸς καὶ υἱὸς τῆς παιδίσκης σου (hoti egō doulos sos kai huios tēs paidiskēs sou)

a: modeled on the holy tent you made ready at the beginning
t: A copy of the heavenly tent
p: The temple copies a holy tent God prepared from the beginning, the heavenly model Moses was shown.
b: Moses was told to make the tabernacle by "the pattern you are being shown on the mountain" (Exodus 25:40; compare Exodus 25:9). Wisdom says the temple and altar are a mimēma, a copy, of a holy tent prepared "from the beginning," that is, in heaven before the world. Hebrews makes the same argument about the earthly sanctuary: "What they serve is a copy and a shadow of the things in heaven" (Hebrews 8:5), and Christ went into "heaven itself" (Hebrews 9:24). The writer uses naos for the temple, the word for the sanctuary building, and skēnē, "tent," the Greek Bible's word for the tabernacle.
orig: μίμημα σκηνῆς ἁγίας ἣν προητοίμασας ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς (mimēma skēnēs hagias hēn proētoimasas ap' archēs)
r: Exodus 25:9; Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:24; Acts 7:44; 1 Kings 5:5

a: she was present when you were making the world
p: Proverbs 8 says Wisdom was there when God set the heavens in place; the prayer repeats it.
b: "I was there when he fixed the heavens in place" (Proverbs 8:27), says Wisdom in Proverbs, and "I was at his side, a craftsman" (Proverbs 8:30). The prayer adds that she knows what pleases God "and what your commands count as right," linking Wisdom to God's law, as Sirach links her to the Torah (Sirach 24:23). John says of the Word, "In the beginning, this one was with God" (John 1:2).

a: For what human being can know God's plan?
t: Who knows the mind of the Lord?
p: The question echoes Isaiah 40:13, which Paul quotes in Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16.
b: "Who has taken the measure of the LORD's Spirit? / What adviser of his has taught him anything?" (Isaiah 40:13). Paul quotes the Greek of Isaiah: "For who has come to know the Lord's mind? Or who has been his adviser?" (Romans 11:34). Wisdom's answer in 9:17 is the same as Paul's in 1 Corinthians 2:10–16: no one, unless God gives his Spirit.

a: For a perishable body is a weight on the soul
t: Does the body drag the soul down?
p: It sounds like Plato. Augustine quoted it often: the body's corruption, not the body, is the weight.
b: Plato's Socrates says "the corporeal is burdensome and heavy and earthy," and that a soul attached to it "is weighed down" (Phaedo 81c). Wisdom's "perishable body," "earthly tent" and "weight" use the same picture. Readings: (1) The writer takes over Plato's view that the body is a burden to the soul (many historians). (2) The writer speaks of the body as it is now, perishable, not of the body as such. Augustine took this second view and quoted the verse again and again: the soul is burdened "not by any body whatsoever, but by the body such as it has become in consequence of sin" (City of God 13.16; also 12.15; 14.3; Confessions 7.17.23). Paul uses the tent picture for the same groaning: "While we are in this tent we groan under the weight" (2 Corinthians 5:4).
orig: φθαρτὸν γὰρ σῶμα βαρύνει ψυχήν, καὶ βρίθει τὸ γεῶδες σκῆνος νοῦν πολυφρόντιδα (phtharton gar sōma barynei psychēn, kai brithei to geōdes skēnos noun polyphrontida)

a: this earthly tent
t: Compared with the Bible: the body as a tent
p: Paul and Peter call the body a tent; Wisdom shares the picture, but its 'weight on the soul' goes beyond them.
b: Agrees in the picture: "We know that if the earthly house we live in, this tent, is torn down, we have from God a building" (2 Corinthians 5:1); Peter speaks of "while I am still in this tent" (2 Peter 1:13). Goes beyond in its stress: Paul does not long to be rid of the body: "It is not that we want to be undressed, but to be dressed over, so that life may swallow up what is mortal" (2 Corinthians 5:4), and he hopes for the body's resurrection. Wisdom says nothing of a resurrection of the body. Augustine read the verse of the body as it now is, after sin (see the note above), which brings it closer to Paul; read as Plato's burden of the body as such, it stands further from him.

a: sent your Holy Spirit down from the heights
p: The prayer sets God's Wisdom beside his Holy Spirit as one gift. The Plain English Translation capitalizes Spirit here, as for God's Spirit.
b: "Unless you gave wisdom / and sent your Holy Spirit": the two lines say the same thing twice, as Hebrew poetry does. The book calls Wisdom "a spirit that loves people" (1:6) and "the Lord's spirit" fills the world (1:7). In the Hebrew Bible the phrase "holy spirit" occurs only in Psalm 51:11 and Isaiah 63:10–11. Read with the New Testament, this is the Holy Spirit given from on high (Luke 24:49; John 14:26); read within the Jewish Bible, it is God's own power and presence, not a separate person. The site capitalizes "Spirit" for God's Spirit, by context.
orig: καὶ ἔπεμψας τὸ ἅγιόν σου πνεῦμα ἀπὸ ὑψίστων (kai epempsas to hagion sou pneuma apo hypsistōn)

a: and Wisdom saved them
p: The prayer ends on 'saved by wisdom', and chapter 10 shows how, from Adam to the Exodus.
b: The last word of the prayer, esōthēsan, "they were saved," is the theme of the rest of the book. Chapter 10 tells how Wisdom saved seven righteous people and Israel, and chapters 11 to 19 tell how God saved Israel and punished Egypt. The book can be divided here: chapters 6 to 9 praise Wisdom, and chapters 10 to 19 show her, and God, at work in history.

a: She guarded the first-formed father of the world
p: Chapter 10 tells the story from Adam to Moses without naming anyone. Each hero is 'a righteous man'.
b: The chapter is built on the word "She" (hautē), which begins its main sentences (10:1, 10:5, 10:6, 10:10, 10:13, 10:15). Seven righteous people are saved by Wisdom: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jacob, Joseph and Moses (with Israel). Each is set against a wicked counterpart: Cain, the generation of Babel, the cities of the plain, Esau, Joseph's accusers, Egypt. No one is named; the reader who knows Genesis and Exodus fills in the names. The effect is to turn the stories into patterns: wisdom saves, folly destroys. Hebrews 11 builds a similar list on faith.

a: pulled him out of his own trespass
t: Compared with the Bible: Adam rescued
p: Genesis does not say that Adam was rescued from his sin. Wisdom says so, and goes beyond Genesis.
b: Goes beyond. Genesis tells of Adam's sin, God's judgment and the sending out of the garden (Genesis 3:17–24), and of God making garments of skin for the man and woman (Genesis 3:21), but says nothing of Adam's repentance or rescue. Wisdom says Wisdom "pulled him out of his own trespass" and gave him the power to rule (Genesis 1:28). Jewish and Christian tradition later told of Adam's repentance (the Life of Adam and Eve, a writing in no church's Bible). Paraptōma, "trespass," is Paul's word for Adam's sin in Romans 5:15–18.

a: he was destroyed together with the fury in which he killed his brother
t: Compared with the Bible: Cain perished
p: Genesis says Cain lived on and built a city. Wisdom says he 'was destroyed', which may mean a ruin of the soul.
b: Goes beyond, and seems to conflict. In Genesis Cain is protected by a mark, has a son and builds a city (Genesis 4:15–17). Wisdom says he "was destroyed" (synapōleto, "perished together with") with his murderous rage. One reading takes this as spiritual ruin: by leaving Wisdom he lost the true life, as the ungodly in 1:12–16 "invite death." The verb can also mean being lost along with something. Cain is the first "unrighteous man" of the chapter, the opposite of Abel the righteous (Genesis 4:8; 1 John 3:12).

a: When the earth was flooded because of him
t: Compared with the Bible: the Flood because of Cain
p: Genesis blames the Flood on human violence in general; Wisdom traces it to Cain.
b: Goes beyond. Genesis 6:5–13 says the earth was full of violence and every plan of the human heart was evil. Wisdom traces that violence back to Cain, the first murderer: "because of him" the earth was flooded. The "righteous man" is Noah, whom Genesis calls "righteous" (Genesis 6:9), saved "on a worthless bit of wood," the ark (Genesis 6:14). Wisdom calls the ark wood again in 14:5–7, where it says "blessed is the wood"; see that note.

a: When the nations were thrown into confusion
p: The 'confusion' of the nations is Babel (Genesis 11); the righteous man is Abraham, called out of it.
b: The Greek synchythentōn, "confused," recalls Babel, where "the LORD mixed up the speech of all the earth" (Genesis 11:9). Their "agreement in wickedness" is the one language and one plan of Genesis 11:1–6. Wisdom then "found" Abraham, who comes right after Babel in Genesis (Genesis 11:27–12:3). The last line is the binding of Isaac: Wisdom kept Abraham strong against his love for "your son, please, your only one, whom you love" (Genesis 22:2).

a: his deep love for his child
p: Splanchna, 'inner parts', is the seat of tender feeling: Abraham's love for Isaac, which Wisdom made him strong against.
b: The Greek speaks of Abraham's splanchna for his child, the gut feeling of a parent's love. The Bible says Abraham did not hold back his son (Genesis 22:12, 22:16); Wisdom adds that he did not do it without a struggle, but by a strength God gave. James and Hebrews read the same test as the proof of Abraham's faith (James 2:21–23; Hebrews 11:17–19).
orig: ἐπὶ τέκνου σπλάγχνοις (epi teknou splanchnois)

a: the Five Cities
p: Genesis names five cities of the plain; Wisdom calls them the Five Cities, though Zoar was spared.
b: Genesis 14:2 lists five cities: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (Zoar). Lot fled to Zoar, which God did not overthrow (Genesis 19:20–23). So when Wisdom speaks of "the fire falling from above on the Five Cities" (Greek Pentapolis), the name stands for the region, not for five cities burned. Josephus too speaks of "the traces [or shadows] of the five cities" still to be seen there (Jewish War 4.484). The "righteous man" is Lot, whom 2 Peter also calls righteous: "Lot, though, was righteous, and God rescued him" (2 Peter 2:7).

a: plants whose fruit never fully ripens
p: Visitors to the Dead Sea told of fruit that looked ripe but turned to smoke and ash. Josephus reports it.
b: The land around the Dead Sea, with its salt, bitumen and sulfur springs, struck ancient visitors as a burned land. Josephus, describing the region in the first century AD, says the remains of the divine fire can still be seen there, and of the fruits that grow there, "if you pluck them with your hands, they dissolve into smoke and ashes" (Jewish War 4.484). The Greek says the plants bear fruit "in seasons that never come to their end" (atelesin hōrais): the fruit never ripens. Wisdom points to the smoking land, the false fruit and the pillar of salt as standing witnesses.
orig: ἀτελέσιν ὥραις καρποφοροῦντα φυτά (atelesin hōrais karpophorounta phyta)

a: the monument of a soul that would not believe
p: The pillar of salt is Lot's wife, who looked back (Genesis 19:26). Jesus said, 'Remember Lot's wife!'
b: "His wife, coming behind him, looked back, and she turned into a pillar of salt" (Genesis 19:26). Wisdom calls hers "a soul that would not believe": she did not trust the warning not to look back (Genesis 19:17). Jesus uses her as a warning for the day of the Son of Man: "Remember Lot's wife!" (Luke 17:32).

a: She let him see God's kingdom
p: Fleeing Esau, Jacob dreamed of a stairway to heaven. Wisdom calls this seeing 'God's kingdom'.
b: Jacob fled from his brother's anger (Genesis 27:41–45) and at Bethel "dreamed, and look: a stairway set up on the earth, its top reaching the sky, and look: angels of God going up and going down on it" (Genesis 28:12). Wisdom calls this vision "the kingdom of God," God reigning in heaven among his angels, and "holy things" (or "holy ones," the angels; one codex reads "human beings"). Jesus tells Nathanael he will see "God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man" (John 1:51).

a: She was the judge of his hard match and gave him the prize
p: Brabeuō means to umpire a contest and award the prize; the 'hard match' is Jacob's wrestling at the Jabbok.
b: The verb brabeuō comes from brabeion, the prize at the games (Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 9:24 and Philippians 3:14). The "hard match" is Jacob's night of wrestling at the Jabbok, where he was told, "you have struggled with God and with humans and have won" (Genesis 32:28). Wisdom draws the moral in Greek terms: Jacob learned that eusebeia, "godliness," is stronger than anything. The enemies and ambushes are probably Laban and Esau (Genesis 31; 33), though the verse names no one.
orig: ἀγῶνα ἰσχυρὸν ἐβράβευσεν αὐτῷ (agōna ischyron ebrabeusen autō)

a: She pulled him out of sin
p: The 'sin' Joseph was rescued from is the temptation of Potiphar's wife (Genesis 39). The Latin reads 'from sinners'.
b: Joseph refused his master's wife: "How could I do this great evil and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). Wisdom says she kept him from that sin, then went down with him into the "pit," the prison (Genesis 39:20; 40:15), until he received authority over Egypt (Genesis 41:40–44). The Vulgate reads a peccatoribus, "from sinners," which shifts the sense to his brothers and his accusers; see the variant.

a: She went down with him into the pit
p: Lakkos is a pit or cistern. Genesis calls both the pit Joseph was thrown into and his prison by that name.
b: Lakkos is a cistern or pit. It fits both the dry pit his brothers threw him into (Genesis 37:24) and the prison in Egypt, which Joseph himself calls "this pit" (Genesis 40:15; compare Genesis 41:14). Wisdom joins both: she went down with him, as God "was with Joseph" in prison (Genesis 39:21). The plural "scepters of a kingdom" is the royal authority Pharaoh gave him.
orig: συνκατέβη αὐτῷ εἰς λάκκον (synkatebē autō eis lakkon)

a: She went into the soul of the Lord's servant
p: Therapōn, 'attendant', is the word Hebrews 3:5 uses for Moses when it echoes Numbers 12:7.
b: "Not so my servant Moses. / In all my house he is faithful" (Numbers 12:7). Hebrews echoes that verse with the same word, therapōn, a trusted attendant: "Moses was faithful in the whole of God's house as an attendant" (Hebrews 3:5). Wisdom says Wisdom herself entered Moses' soul (compare 7:27). The "fearsome kings" are Pharaoh (the plural may include his officials), whom Moses faced with "wonders and signs" (Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 34:11).
orig: εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ψυχὴν θεράποντος Κυρίου (eisēlthen eis psychēn therapontos Kyriou)

a: She paid the holy ones the wages of their labor
p: The silver and gold the Israelites took from Egypt are read as back pay for their years of slave labor.
b: "They had asked Egypt for silver things and gold things and clothing" (Exodus 12:35), "So they stripped Egypt bare" (Exodus 12:36). Wisdom explains this as fair wages: the slaves were paid at last for their labor. "A covering ... by day and a flame ... at night" is the pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21), here made one of Wisdom's own forms.

a: She took them across the Red Sea
t: Red Sea or Sea of Reeds
p: The Greek says 'Red Sea', as the Septuagint does; the Hebrew of Exodus has Yam Suf, the 'Sea of Reeds'.
b: The Hebrew of Exodus calls the sea Yam Suf, which the site's Old Testament translates "Sea of Reeds." The Septuagint, and Wisdom after it, say thalassa erythra, "Red Sea," the Greek name for the waters south of Egypt and Arabia. The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek name here. On where the crossing took place, see the topic on the sea of reeds.
orig: θάλασσαν ἐρυθράν (thalassan erythran)

a: she threw them up out of the depths of the abyss
p: Exodus says Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore. Josephus tells of their weapons washing up for Israel.
b: "Israel saw Egypt dead on the shore of the sea" (Exodus 14:30). Wisdom says that she "threw them up out of the depths," and then "the righteous stripped the ungodly" (10:20). Josephus tells a related story: "Moses gathered together the weapons of the Egyptians, which were brought to the camp of the Hebrews by the current of the sea" (Jewish Antiquities 2.349), seeing divine providence in it. Wisdom speaks only of spoils, not of weapons, so whether it knew the same story cannot be shown.

a: gave clear speech to the tongues of infants
t: Even babies sang at the sea
p: A later Jewish teaching says that at the sea even infants sang the Song of Moses. The Talmud quotes Psalm 8 for it.
b: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) was sung by all Israel. A teaching of Rabbi Yose the Galilean in the Babylonian Talmud says that when Israel came up out of the sea, a baby on its mother's lap and an infant at the breast saw the Divine Presence and sang, "This is my God, and I will honor him" (Exodus 15:2), citing Psalm 8: "Out of the mouths of children and babies at the breast / you have founded a strong defense" (Psalm 8:2; Bavli Sotah 30b). A similar idea appears later in this teaching; whether it comes from this verse or from a tradition both share is not known. "Those who could not speak" may also recall Moses, "heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue" (Exodus 4:10). Jesus quotes Psalm 8 when children praise him in the temple (Matthew 21:16).
